3.1 Gene selection for the reference

Bastien Chassagnol

9 Nov 2026

Source: vignettes/03-1-feature-selection.qmd

Scope

This chapter states which genes should enter a DeCovarT reference built from single-cell data, and why. It holds the theory: what the genes are for, the selection strategies of the literature, four tiers of selection, and the statistical tests and tail bounds behind them (Gaspard-Boulinc et al. 2025; Avila Cobos et al. 2018). The reference considered here is a single-cell experiment on one specimen. Cross-cell consistency (tier ii, Section 3) uses that reference alone; cross-platform consistency (tier iii, Section 4) also needs a bulk sample that matches it. Cross-sample consistency, references from other technologies, dependent cells and covariance-driven selection are perspectives (Section 7). The application to a real reference (filters as applied, settings, rank tables, code) is in the feature-selection chapter of the reproducibility book. Strategies compared on simulated references are in Appendix S6. Marker-based abundance scores (enrichment modules) are out of scope (Aran et al. 2017).

Local symbols. C=\sum_jC_j is the number of reference cells in one time slot, and j(c) is the label of cell c. v_{gj} is the g-th diagonal entry of \boldsymbol{V}_j. A gene panel is written \mathcal{G}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,G\}. In the review, \mu_{gj} is the mean of gene g in type j on the scale of the method at hand, u_{gj} its type share and k a rank (Equation 1). In the count models, m_{gc}=\operatorname{E}(x_{gc}) is the mean of gene g in cell c, V(m)=m+m^{2}/\psi_g the negative-binomial (NB) variance function, \mathcal{D}_g(M) the deviance of model M, \Lambda_g the likelihood-ratio statistic, R^{2}_{D,g} the deviance explained, r_{gc} the raw Pearson residual, r^{\mathrm{SP}}_{gc} the standardised one, \hat\phi_g the Pearson dispersion and h_{gc} the leverage of cell c (Section 3.1, Section 4.1). For the bulk filter, \tilde\mu_{gj} is the expected count of gene g in one cell of type j, \hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj} its average over the C_j reference cells, \sigma^{2}_{gj}=\tilde\mu_{gj}+\tilde\mu_{gj}^{2}/\psi_g the per-cell NB variance, \delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g the distance of the bulk to the range of the reference means, D_{gi} the plug-in discrepancy, h_g the leverage of gene g and \tau_g^{2} its residual variance, S_M the standardised sum over a gene module M, K_D(u) the cumulant generating function of D with argument u, and \chi_G the number of classes of a colouring of a gene graph (Section 4.2). \eta_1,\dots,\eta_4 are the parameters of the sub-exponential properties, and \gamma,\gamma' absolute constants (Note 1, Note 3). B is the number of permutations (Section 3.2.1).

Warning 1: What the genes are for

The target is a set of genes that makes the reference moments (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}) estimable and informative about \boldsymbol{p}. This is not population-level differential expression, for two reasons.

  • One specimen. The reference is one technical scRNA-seq experiment. Its cells are draws from one specimen, not biological replicates, so every p-value below calibrates a screen inside that specimen. Treating cells as replicates of a population contrast inflates the false discoveries (Zimmerman et al. 2021; Squair et al. 2021; Crowell et al. 2020). Only the within-donor covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} is estimable; the between-donor part needs R\ge2 donors (2.1).
  • Labels are given. A test of the type effect is valid only if the labels were fixed before the statistic is computed. Labels obtained by clustering the same matrix make the test anti-conservative (post-clustering inference, González-Delgado et al. 2025) TODO-cite: González-Delgado et al. 2025, post-clustering inference; key gonzalezDelgadoPostclusteringInference2025 exists in the book bib only.

Selection proceeds in four tiers (Figure 1):

  1. quality control, prior-knowledge markers and a presence gate (Section 2);
  2. cross-cell consistency: tests of the type effect used as a gate, then an effect-size rank (Section 3);
  3. cross-platform consistency between the reference and a matched bulk: influence diagnostics and a bulk filter (Section 4);
  4. down-weighting by the model instead of removal (Section 5).

Tiers (i) to (iii) are filters; tier (iv) is part of the likelihood. Feature selection as a pre-modelling filter has the usual caveats (Guyon and Elisseeff 2003): it is a proposal, to be checked by out-of-sample deconvolution error (S6).

1 Review of gene-selection strategies used by deconvolution algorithms

Deconvolution methods choose genes in three ways:

  • univariate one-versus-others screens (Section 1.1): differential-expression and fold-change ranks (Section 1.1.1), the ANOVA F statistic (Section 1.1.2) and specificity scores (Section 1.1.3);
  • searches over the whole signature (Section 1.2);
  • no selection, with gene weights doing the work (Section 5).

This section reviews them, states where they depart from the count model used here (Section 1.3), and compares second-generation methods in Table 1. Each method’s likelihood is reviewed in 5.1.

1.1 Univariate screens, one versus others

Classical signature pipelines score gene g for type j against the remaining types, then concatenate the per-type shortlists (Abbas et al. 2009; Newman et al. 2015; Finotello et al. 2019).

1.1.1 Differential-expression and fold-change ranks

limma–voom, edgeR and DESeq2 are the usual tools for one-versus-rest contrasts (Ritchie et al. 2015; Robinson et al. 2010; Love et al. 2014). CIBERSORT keeps genes with adjusted p\le0.3, orders them by fold change and prunes the panel by its condition number (Newman et al. 2015). Abbas et al. keep genes whose expression in the target type exceeds that of the second- and third-ranked types, then choose the panel with the smallest condition number (Abbas et al. 2009). On cells of one specimen these tests treat cells as replicates (Warning 1); their pseudo-bulk versions need donors (Section 7.1).

1.1.2 ANOVA F statistic

Wang et al. rank genes by the F statistic of a type factor against an intercept-only model (Wang et al. 2010). This is one omnibus test per gene instead of one test per type. Its count-model versions, and their calibration, are the tests of tier (ii) (Section 3.2).

1.1.3 Specificity scores

Long one-versus-rest lists are often compacted with the Shannon entropy or the Gini coefficient of the type shares u_{gj}=\mu_{gj}/\sum_{\ell}\mu_{g\ell}, as in BioQC (Zhang et al. 2017):

H_g=-\sum_{j=1}^{J}u_{gj}\log u_{gj}, \qquad \mathrm{Gini}_g = \frac{1}{2J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\lvert u_{gj}-u_{g\ell}\rvert = \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^{J}(2R_{gj}-J-1)\,u_{gj}, \tag{1}

with 0\log0=0; R_{gj}=R(u_{gj}) is the rank of u_{gj} among the J shares of gene g, and u_{g(1)}\le\cdots\le u_{g(J)} are its order statistics, so that u_{g(R_{gj})}=u_{gj} (rank-based notation of Jaeckel and of Hettmansperger and McKean). H_g/\log J and J\,\mathrm{Gini}_g/(J-1) lie in [0,1]; low entropy and high Gini mean that few types carry the mass. Figure 2 derives the Gini coefficient in five steps, from the mean absolute difference of the type means to the share form of Equation 1. The pairwise and sorted forms agree because, the share of rank R_{gj} is larger than R_{gj}-1 shares and smaller than J-R_{gj} shares, so it enters the double sum with the net weight 2R_{gj}-J-1. Both scores reward exclusive expression, which the presence gate (Section 2.2) excludes, and neither sees redundancy between genes.

For the two genes of Figure 2 the Gini coefficients are 21/200=0.105 and 77/100=0.770, and the corrected values J\,\mathrm{Gini}_g/(J-1) are 3/25 and 22/25. A gene expressed in one type only has u_{g(J)}=1, so Equation 1 gives (J-1)/J, the maximum.

Concatenation does not control redundancy. Two specific markers of different types can still be nearly collinear rows of \boldsymbol{\mu} when the types share a programme (a lineage, an activation axis), so the union of per-type lists inflates |\mathcal{G}| while \kappa_2(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}) stays large and NNLS or GLS fits stay unstable (Newman et al. 2015; Avila Cobos et al. 2018). A criterion on the whole signature is then needed.

1.2 Searches over the whole signature

  • Condition number. CIBERSORT and DWLS keep the candidate signature with the smallest \kappa_2(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}) (Newman et al. 2015; Tsoucas et al. 2019, 7; Gong and Szustakowski 2013); its limits are in
  • Multi-objective genetic search. AutoGeneS searches gene subsets with a genetic algorithm that minimises the correlation between type centroids and maximises their distance (Aliee and Theis 2021); MOGAMUN applies the same kind of search to network modules (Novoa-del-Toro et al. 2021). The loss is defined on the full J-column signature, not on one-versus-rest lists.

Both criteria see the means only. Criteria that also use the within-type covariance need \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}, so they come after tier (ii) (Section 7.4).

1.3 Critiques of current marker rules

The reviewed marker rules (Table 1) depart from the count model of tier (ii) in five ways.

  • Hurdle models on droplet counts. DWLS defines markers with the MAST hurdle model (Tsoucas et al. 2019, 7). Droplet UMI counts show no zero inflation beyond what the NB predicts (Svensson 2020) TODO-cite: Svensson 2020, Droplet scRNA-seq is not zero-inflated, Nat. Biotechnol., doi:10.1038/s41587-019-0379-5, and current data do not support zero-inflated measurement models (Sarkar and Stephens 2021, 5). The hurdle splits one count into a detection and a magnitude test (Finak et al. 2015) TODO-cite: Finak et al. 2015, MAST, Genome Biol., doi:10.1186/s13059-015-0844-5 where one NB test of Equation 6 suffices.
  • Gaussian t-tests on counts. ReDeconv uses a two-sample t-test between cells (Lu et al. 2025, 14); deMixSC uses a paired t-test of bulk against matched pseudo-bulk (Guo et al. 2023, 12).
  • Cells as independent replicates. Every test above that runs on cells (DWLS, ReDeconv, BayesPrism’s marker option) treats them as replicates of a population contrast (Warning 1). Pseudo-bulk DESeq2, edgeR or limma–voom avoid this only with biological replicates at the level of the contrast (Section 7.1).
  • No multiplicity control. ReDeconv keeps genes with p<0.05 in each comparison against every other type, with no FDR correction (Lu et al. 2025, 14).
  • Graph-based screens before the graph is estimated. Differential-network screens (INDEED, D-trace) and Markov-boundary growth of marker seeds need fitted graphs; here they are post hoc (Section 7.4.6).

1.4 Comparison of second-generation methods

Table 1 summarises, method by method, the facts found in the papers, with the columns in the order of the tiers. Page numbers refer to the PDF pages of the local extractions (“supp.” marks a supplement). A dash means that the item was not found in the extracted text; it does not mean that the method has no such step. The same facts are in Appendix C of the CardamomOT comparison note.

TODO-cite: Maugé & Ventre 2026, CardamomOT, PLoS Comput. Biol. 22(10):e1014838, doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014838

DeCovarT builds on these methods in three ways.

  • Covariance in the criterion. Only DeCovarT puts gene–gene covariance into the criterion that estimates \boldsymbol{p}; DECALS and MEAD use it only for the variance of their estimators. The other methods treat genes as independent, the setting in which a univariate screen is also the objective (Section 7.4.1). DeCovarT keeps the univariate screen as a gate (tier ii) and leaves the weighting to the covariance (tier iv).
  • One count test per gene. The tests that select genes run on cells, mostly with Gaussian or hurdle models, and only DWLS (markers) and deMixSC (platform discrepancy) report a multiplicity correction. DeCovarT uses one test of the type effect per gene, chosen among four with known assumptions, and a Benjamini–Hochberg gate (Section 3.2).
  • No perfect markers. MuSiC and MEAD argue against marker pre-selection when the genes are weighted, and MEAD shows that perfect markers break identifiability under gene-wise platform ratios (Section 4); DWLS and DECALS still build marker-only signatures. DeCovarT removes perfect markers with the presence gate and weights the remaining genes.

2 Tier (i): quality control and prior knowledge

QC removes cells and genes that lie outside the support of any expression model. The thresholds below are examples from the reviewed methods (Table 1), not defaults of DeCovarT.

  • Cells. Library size more than 3 median absolute deviations (MAD) from the median of its type, and cells more than 3 MAD from the median pairwise distance within their type (RNA-Sieve, optional; Erdmann-Pham et al. (2021), supplement p. 3). Fewer than 500 UMIs, fewer than 200 detected genes, or more than 50 % mitochondrial UMIs (deMixSC; Guo et al. (2023), p. 11).
  • Genes. Ribosomal, mitochondrial and sex-chromosome genes, which reflect cell survival and donor sex rather than type (BayesPrism; Chu et al. (2022), supplement pp. 14, 19). Genes detected in fewer than 20 % of the cells of every type (RNA-Sieve, supplement p. 3).

2.1 Prior-knowledge markers

A short curated list of markers (lineage or signalling genes named by the biology of the tissue) enters as hard prior knowledge. These genes are kept whatever their rank in tier (ii), provided they pass the presence gate, and they are reported as a separate group. Two rules keep the list honest. It is fixed before the data-driven ranks are seen. It is never used to score the data-driven panel, since a panel judged by its overlap with the markers that were forced into it is judged by construction. The overlap between the curated list and the genes that the data-driven tiers keep can be reported as a description, for example with a hypergeometric tail, as the reproducibility book does.

2.2 Presence gate in every type

Necessary, not sufficient

A gene enters tier (ii) only if

\min_{j}\delta_{gj}\ge\delta_{\min} \quad\text{and}\quad \min_{j}v_{gj}>0, \tag{2}

with \delta_{\min} a few per cent (for example 0.05), fixed before the ranks are seen. These are necessary conditions for a non-singular within-type covariance and for an identifiable \boldsymbol{p}; they are not sufficient. Two cases show what the gate excludes.

  • Zero in every cell of type j. Then v_{gj}=0 and the whole row and column g of \boldsymbol{V}_j are zero: \boldsymbol{V}_j is singular (\det\boldsymbol{V}_j=0), the correlation v_{gh}/\sqrt{v_{gg}v_{hh}} is 0/0 and so undefined, and the fitted type-j Gaussian is degenerate, a point mass in coordinate g. Its likelihood is unbounded, so no maximum-likelihood estimate exists.
  • Detected in a single cell c. With count a in that cell, the centred counts of g are a(\boldsymbol{e}_c-\mathbf{1}/C_j), and its correlation with any gene h is r_{gh}=\tilde h_c/(\sqrt{1-1/C_j}\,\lVert\tilde{\boldsymbol h}\rVert), \tilde{\boldsymbol h} the centred counts of h: one cell sets it. Two genes detected only in cell c have r=1 whatever their counts, a perfect and degenerate correlation, and \boldsymbol{V}_j is again singular.

With \delta_{\min}C_j\ge2 the gate keeps only genes with at least two non-zero cells in every type, which excludes both cases. It does not make \boldsymbol{V}_j invertible: \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{V}_j\le \min(C_j-1,G), so \boldsymbol{V}_j is singular whenever G\ge C_j or genes satisfy an exact linear relation, and shrinkage is still needed (3.2). Nor does it make \boldsymbol{p} identifiable, which requires a non-singular Fisher information for \boldsymbol{p} (1.2). The gate also removes perfect markers, whose effect under gene-wise platform ratios is in Section 4.

3 Tier (ii): cross-cell consistency

MuSiC introduced “marker gene consistency” with two parts (Wang et al. 2019, 2). Cross-cell consistency asks whether a gene is stable across the cells of one type, so that biased cell capture does not drive its selection; cross-cell consistent genes have a low within-cluster variance (Wang et al. 2019, 3). Cross-sample consistency asks whether a gene’s type mean is stable across specimens (MuSiC’s cross-subject consistency), and needs at least two of them. With a reference from one specimen only cross-cell consistency can be assessed from the reference alone; cross-sample consistency is a perspective (Section 7.1), and consistency with a matched bulk is tier (iii) (Section 4). The natural statistic for cross-cell consistency splits a gene’s variation into between-type and within-type parts.

3.1 Count null model and Pearson residuals

The technical null fits each gene with library size as the only covariate,

M_{0}:\; \log m_{gc}=\beta_{0g}+\log s_{c}, \qquad x_{gc}\sim\mathrm{NB}(m_{gc},\psi_{g}), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(x_{gc})=V(m_{gc})=m_{gc}+\frac{m_{gc}^{2}}{\psi_g}. \tag{3}

M_0 is fitted gene by gene with our own NB GLM, with \psi_g estimated per gene by maximum likelihood (for example with glmGamPoi (Ahlmann-Eltze and Huber 2020) or MASS::glm.nb()), and its residuals are not clipped1

The raw Pearson residual is

r_{gc}=\frac{x_{gc}-\hat m_{gc}}{\sqrt{V(\hat m_{gc})}}, \qquad r^{\mathrm{SP}}_{gc}=\frac{r_{gc}}{\sqrt{\hat\phi_g\,(1-h_{gc})}}, \tag{4}

and r^{\mathrm{SP}}_{gc} is the standardised Pearson residual (Agresti 2015). \hat\phi_g is the Pearson dispersion (the sum of squared r_{gc} divided by the residual degrees of freedom), and h_{gc} the leverage of cell c in the weighted hat matrix of the final IRLS step. The factor 1-h_{gc} corrects for a fitted value that a high-leverage cell partly sets itself. SCTransform residuals are raw residuals: they carry neither \hat\phi_g nor 1-h_{gc}, and they are clipped. Standardised does not mean Gaussian: at low means Pearson residuals stay discrete and skewed, and randomised quantile residuals (Dunn & Smyth 1996) TODO-cite: Dunn & Smyth 1996, Randomized quantile residuals, J. Comput. Graph. Stat. 5(3):236-244, doi:10.1080/10618600.1996.10474708 are the residuals to compare with a normal reference.

The raw residuals of M_0 split as

\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{B},g} = \sum_{j=1}^{J}C_{j}\bigl(\bar r_{gj}-\bar r_{g}\bigr)^{2}, \qquad \mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{W},g} = \sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{c:j(c)=j}\bigl(r_{gc}-\bar r_{gj}\bigr)^{2}, \tag{5}

with \bar r_{gj} the mean residual in type j and \bar r_{g} the overall mean (\approx0). A lineage marker has a large between-type and a small within-type part; a stress-response gene can have a large total residual variance and still a small between-type part. The sums weight every cell equally, so the abundant types dominate them; tests that allow a different variance per type are in Section 3.2.1. Figure 3 shows the steps of the null model on simulated counts.

3.2 Four tests of the type effect

Add the type main effect to Equation 3:

M_{1}:\; \log m_{gc}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_{g,j(c)}+\log s_{c}, \qquad \beta_{g1}=0, \qquad H_{0g}:\beta_{g2}=\cdots=\beta_{gJ}=0 . \tag{6}

The joint null has J-1 degrees of freedom (Agresti 2015). One omnibus test per gene replaces \binom{J}{2} pairwise or J one-versus-rest tests, and a single Benjamini–Hochberg correction across genes follows. Four tests of H_{0g} are compared (Table 2). The presence gate removes the all-zero types near which the Wald test fails (Hauck–Donner effect; Yee (2022)), so the Wald test is not used.

  • Likelihood ratio (analysis of deviance). \Lambda_g=\mathcal{D}_g(M_0)-\mathcal{D}_g(M_1), with both models fitted at the \hat\psi_g of M_1, referred to \chi^2_{J-1}. It needs one M_1 fit per gene, a one-way GLM with J coefficients.
  • One-way ANOVA F on variance-stabilised counts. The shifted logarithm \log(x_{gc}/s_c+y_0), with y_0=\psi_0/4 for a typical dispersion \psi_0, stabilises the NB variance and performs as well as more elaborate transformations in a published benchmark (Ahlmann-Eltze & Huber 2023) TODO-cite: Ahlmann-Eltze & Huber 2023, Comparison of transformations for single-cell RNA-seq data, Nat. Methods 20, doi:10.1038/s41592-023-01814-1. The F statistic of the type factor on these values is referred to F_{J-1,C-J} (Wang et al. 2010). When the variance on the transformed scale still differs between types, Welch’s heteroscedastic one-way test (Welch 1951) TODO-cite: Welch 1951, On the comparison of several mean values: an alternative approach, Biometrika 38:330-336 is the fallback.
  • Quasi-likelihood F. Defined below (Equation 7).
  • Permutation calibration. Welch’s statistic on the residuals of M_0, referred to a permutation distribution (Section 3.2.1).

Quasi-likelihood F. Dividing \Lambda_g/(J-1) by the Pearson dispersion of M_1 gives

F_{g} = \frac{\Lambda_g/(J-1)}{\hat\phi_g}, \qquad \hat\phi_g=\frac{1}{C-J}\sum_{c}\frac{(x_{gc}-\hat m^{(1)}_{gc})^{2}}{V(\hat m^{(1)}_{gc})}, \tag{7}

with \hat m^{(1)}_{gc} the fitted means of M_1, referred to F_{J-1,C-J}. The mean model Equation 6 and the variance function V(m)=m+m^2/\psi_g are kept, and a scalar \phi_g absorbs a variance larger or smaller than V predicts. This is the quasi-likelihood F test of the edgeR pipeline and of glmGamPoi::test_de(), which use the deviance in the numerator and also shrink \hat\phi_g across genes (Lund et al. 2012; Ahlmann-Eltze and Huber 2020). Three consequences follow.

  • Keep overdispersed genes. Within-type overdispersion is the within-type scatter that the denominator already penalises, and the covariance that DeCovarT models. Removing such genes before the test removes that signal.
  • A scalar \phi_g cannot absorb a wrong variance function. Under a Poisson null it cannot absorb the quadratic NB term, whose share grows with the type mean; the pooled \hat\phi_g is then wrong for every type. Use the NB variance, so that \phi_g\approx1 in every type. If the dispersion still differs between types, \hat\phi_g is an average dominated by the large types, and a statistic with one variance per type, Welch’s G referred to permutations, is needed (Section 3.2.1).
  • Gate, then rank by effect size. F_g grows with the counts of a gene as well as with its effect, so it serves as a gate, not as a rank. Genes that pass the FDR gate are ranked by an effect size, the deviance explained R^{2}_{D,g}=1-\mathcal{D}_g(M_1)/\mathcal{D}_g(M_0) or the ratio \mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{B},g}/\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{W},g} of Equation 5, not by p-value.

When the NB variance function itself fails, quasi-likelihood with an empirical variance function is the fallback (Agresti 2015). When the shape differs between types (types that share a mean but differ in dispersion), a location–scale model with type-specific \psi_{gj} tests both, on 2(J-1) degrees of freedom; this is the GAMLSS margin used by scDesign3 (Song et al. 2024), Stasinopoulos & Rigby (2007) TODO-cite: Stasinopoulos & Rigby 2007, GAMLSS in R, J. Stat. Softw. 23(7), doi:10.18637/jss.v023.i07. Whether a dispersion difference should count as a type effect depends on the use: for a gate on mean effects it is a false discovery, while for DeCovarT, which models the within-type covariance, such a gene can still carry information.

3.2.1 Permutation calibration

A permutation null keeps a statistic and replaces its reference distribution by the distribution under random relabelling of the cells.

  • Freedman–Lane. With nuisance covariates (batch, cell line, cell cycle), a global label shuffle creates impossible combinations. The Freedman–Lane scheme fits the reduced model without type, permutes its residuals, adds them back to the reduced fit, refits the full model and recomputes the statistic (Freedman and Lane 1983). In a comparison of permutation strategies for the general linear model, Winkler et al.
    1. write “we recommend the Freedman–Lane and the Smith methods” (p. 393) TODO-cite: Winkler, Ridgway, Webster, Smith & Nichols 2014, Permutation inference for the general linear model, NeuroImage 92:381-397, doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2014.01.060. Here the nuisance part of M_0 is an intercept and the depth offset, so the reduced residuals are the label-free Pearson residuals of M_0, and Freedman–Lane reduces to permuting the labels against them.
  • Welch’s G, not F. Welch’s statistic weights each type mean by C_j over its own within-type variance and corrects the denominator for the estimated variances (Winkler et al. 2014, Eqs 6–7). With one variance group G=F. Under heteroscedasticity F is not pivotal (p. 386): its null distribution then depends on the unknown type-specific variances, and a label permutation does not reproduce them. G stays approximately pivotal, so its permutation p-value remains close to its nominal level.
  • One permutation for all genes. The same B permutations of the cell labels are applied to every gene. Each gene keeps its marginal distribution and its dependence on the other genes; only the link with the label is broken. Shuffling genes, or shuffling within cells, does not produce that null.
  • Smallest p-value. With p_g=(1+\#\{G^{*}_g\ge G_g\})/(B+1), the smallest attainable value is 1/(B+1). For smaller p-values, a generalised Pareto fit to the upper tail of the permutation distribution gives an approximation (Knijnenburg et al. 2009; Winkler et al. 2016) TODO-cite: Knijnenburg, Wessels, Reinders & Shmulevich 2009, Fewer permutations, more accurate P-values, Bioinformatics 25(12):i161-i168, doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btp211 TODO-cite: Winkler, Ridgway, Douaud, Nichols & Smith 2016, Faster permutation inference in brain imaging, NeuroImage 141:502-516, doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2016.05.068.

permuco implements Freedman–Lane for linear models and ANOVA (Frossard & Renaud 2021) TODO-cite: Frossard & Renaud 2021, Permutation tests for regression, ANOVA, and comparison of signals: the permuco package, J. Stat. Softw. 99(15), doi:10.18637/jss.v099.i15. For GLMs, flipscores flips the signs of the score contributions instead of permuting, and stays valid when the variance is misspecified (Hemerik, Goeman & Finos 2020; De Santis et al. 2025) TODO-cite: Hemerik, Goeman & Finos 2020, Robust testing in generalized linear models by sign flipping score contributions, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 82(3), doi:10.1111/rssb.12369 TODO-cite: De Santis et al. 2025, J. Am. Stat. Assoc., doi:10.1080/01621459.2025.2491775. Neither package computes Welch’s G; the figure script below permutes it directly. PERMANOVA is the multivariate sum-of-squares version of the same permutation test (Anderson 2001; vegan::adonis2()) TODO-cite: Anderson 2001, A new method for non-parametric multivariate analysis of variance, Austral Ecol. 26(1):32-46, doi:10.1111/j.1442-9993.2001.01070.pp.x; a module-level version is a perspective (Section 7.4.2).

3.2.2 The four tests on simulated counts

The tests rank genes by the same type effect, so their gene orders should agree; Figure 4 measures how far they do. The simulation has J=4 types of 2,000, 300, 60 and 25 cells and 1,000 genes: 600 nulls with one dispersion per gene, 300 nulls with the same mean in every type but \psi_{gj}=20 in the two large types and 1 in the two small ones, and 100 genes with a type effect.

  • Gene order. Over all genes, Kendall’s \tau_b is 0.98 between the LR and QL F rankings, 0.67 between LR and ANOVA, and 0.73 between LR and the permuted Welch G. Among the 100 alternatives, LR and ANOVA agree more (0.90) and the permuted G less (0.53 to 0.58).
  • Type I error. Under the homoscedastic null all tests reject at most 4.8 % of the genes at 0.05. Under type-specific dispersion, LR, QL F and ANOVA reject 15 % to 19 % of the nulls, and the permuted F on the same residuals 18 %; the permuted G rejects 6 %. QL F behaves like LR because the median \hat\phi_g is 0.999 in both nulls: the pooled dispersion is set by the 2,300 cells of the large types.
  • Power. The permuted G pays for its calibration. With Benjamini–Hochberg at 0.05 it makes 43 discoveries, with an empirical FDR of 0.05 and a power of 0.41; LR makes 105, with an FDR of 0.19 and a power of 0.85. 35 of the 100 alternatives reach the permutation floor 1/(B+1) with B=2{,}000, where the generalised Pareto tail would separate them. Welch’s G referred to its analytic F approximation instead of permutations (not drawn) rejects 11 % of the homoscedastic nulls; the skewness of the residuals of the 25-cell type is a likely cause (not checked).

The trade-off is between a gate that is calibrated when dispersion differs between types (permuted G) and a gate with more power when the NB variance function holds (LR, QL F). Under type-specific dispersion the GAMLSS test above answers a different question, a change in the count law rather than in its mean.

4 Tier (iii): cross-platform consistency

A gene can be a perfect cross-cell marker and still be measured differently by the reference and the bulk protocol. Cross-platform consistency compares the bulk with the single-cell reference, and needs a bulk sample that matches the reference (same tissue, ideally the same specimen). The reviewed methods handle it in four ways.

  • Range bound (RNA-Sieve). Per cell, the expected bulk is a convex combination of the type means, so on a common scale

    \min_{j}\tilde\mu_{gj}\;\le\;\operatorname{E}\tilde y_{g}\;\le\;\max_{j}\tilde\mu_{gj}. \tag{8}

    RNA-Sieve removes genes whose bulk value falls outside this range by more than a sub-Gaussian tail allows (Section 4.2), and genes that are MAD outliers on four summary statistics (largest type mean, largest type standard deviation, largest coefficient of variation, and a bulk-to-reference ratio) (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021, 11, Eqs. 12–13). The bound holds for any weights on the simplex, so it does not depend on whether \boldsymbol{p} or \boldsymbol{q} is the target. A gene-wise platform ratio \tilde b_g far from 1 moves the bulk outside the range; the filter detects that case.

  • Test against a matched benchmark (deMixSC). A paired t-test of real bulk against pseudo-bulk of the same aliquots, with BH at 0.05; the discrepant genes are kept and down-weighted by a fixed factor of 1,000 (Guo et al. 2023, 12).

  • Gene-wise platform ratios in the model. MEAD lets the ratios vary by gene with mean 1 (Xie et al. 2026, 5, 8); RCTD uses a gene-wise platform random effect, estimated once from a pooled pseudo-bulk and then fixed (Cable et al. 2022, 3, 6–7); MuSiC allows a gene- and subject-specific intercept (Wang et al. 2019, 7).

  • Normalisation only. ReDeconv applies gene-length normalisation to the bulk only (Lu et al. 2025, 2).

Gene-wise ratios have a price. MEAD shows that the proportions are not identifiable when all genes are perfect markers and gene-wise ratios are allowed: rescaling the ratios of the markers of type j by a common factor is absorbed by the proportions (Xie et al. 2026, 7). The presence gate (Section 2.2) excludes these genes. Modelling a gene-wise or module-wise scale \tilde b_g inside DeCovarT is a perspective of 5.3.

DeCovarT’s tier (iii) has two parts: influence diagnostics for cells and genes (Section 4.1), and a bulk filter whose thresholds come from tail statements for a discrepancy between the bulk and the reference (Section 4.2).

4.1 Outlier cells and genes: leverage and influence

Residual size, leverage and influence are three different quantities (Agresti 2015). Leverage measures how unusual an observation is in the design, the residual how badly the model predicts its response, and influence how much the fit changes when the observation is removed. Influence needs both.

Cells. In the gene-wise GLM M_1 of Equation 6, leverage belongs to the cells, not to the gene. For a one-way design with a log link the hat value of cell c is

h_{gc}=\frac{w_{gc}}{\sum_{c':\,j(c')=j(c)}w_{gc'}}, \qquad w_{gc}=\frac{\hat m_{gc}^{2}}{V(\hat m_{gc})}, \qquad \mathrm{Cook}_{gc} = \frac{(r^{\mathrm{SP}}_{gc})^{2}}{J}\,\frac{h_{gc}}{1-h_{gc}} = \frac{r_{gc}^{2}\,h_{gc}}{J\,\hat\phi_g\,(1-h_{gc})^{2}}, \tag{9}

with w_{gc} the IRLS weight. The hat values of each type sum to 1, so a cell of a type with C_j cells has h_{gc}\approx1/C_j, and within a type h_{gc} grows with the fitted mean. Every cell of a rare type, and every cell with a large fitted mean, has high leverage. Figure 5 shows the consequence. The 25 cells of the rare high-expression type have leverage near 0.04; the 23 consistent ones have small residuals and a Cook’s distance of at most 0.025. Two doublet-like cells of that type combine that leverage with a residual near 6 and have the largest Cook’s distances, 0.36 and 0.34. Three outliers of the 2,000-cell type have larger residuals, 6.1 to 7.3, but a leverage below 10^{-3}, and their Cook’s distances stay below 0.01. No cell passes the conventional cut of 0.5, and the cut 4/C flags 12 of the 23 consistent rare-type cells on leverage alone.

Genes. At the level of the bulk, the observations are genes: regress the bulk per cell \tilde y_{gi} on the reference signature, the row \hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}}_{g\cdot}, by weighted least squares with weights 1/\tau_g^{2}, \tau_g^{2} the variance of the bulk residual of gene g. With \boldsymbol{X} the G\times J matrix of reference means and \boldsymbol{W}=\operatorname{diag}(1/\tau_g^{2}),

h_g=\frac{\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}}_{g\cdot}^{\top}\bigl(\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{X}\bigr)^{-1}\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}}_{g\cdot}}{\tau_g^{2}}, \qquad \mathrm{Cook}_g=\frac{r_g^{2}}{J}\,\frac{h_g}{1-h_g}, \tag{10}

with r_g the standardised residual of gene g. h_g depends on the scaled row \hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}}_{g\cdot}/\tau_g. When \tau_g grows in proportion to the level of the gene, the level cancels and the leverage follows the direction of the gene’s profile across types, not its level. In Figure 6 the markers of the rarest type and a high-mean gene with a rare-type profile have the highest leverage, 0.024 to 0.044. A gene with a mean 50 times the median and an ordinary profile has a leverage of 0.017, against 0.70 in an unweighted fit. All of these genes have small residuals and a Cook’s distance below 0.021. The ten platform-discordant genes (\tilde b_g=4) have residuals of 2.9 to 10.3; the largest Cook’s distances, 0.48 and 0.33, combine a residual near 10 with a leverage near 0.02. The discordant genes also inflate the residual variance of the fit, from 0.96 to 3.35, which shrinks every standardised residual.

Two rules follow from Table 3 and the two figures. A cell or a gene is flagged only when both its leverage and its standardised residual are large; neither a fixed Cook cut (0.5 or 1 flags nothing in either figure) nor 4/C or 4/G alone separates the injected outliers from consistent high-leverage observations. Rules that shrink by size alone, such as residual clipping or SCDC’s clipping of variance weights at the 15th and 85th percentiles (Dong et al. 2021, 10), shrink the informative high-leverage observations together with the harmful ones.

4.2 Bulk consistency filter

Two statistics compare one bulk sample i with the reference. The first does not need the composition. RNA-Sieve writes its range filter as a probability (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021, Eq. 12, PDF p. 11, Genome Res. p. 1804):

\mathbb{P}\bigl(\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t\bigr), \qquad \delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g =\inf\Bigl\{\lvert\tilde y_{gi}-a\rvert:\ \min_{j}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\le a\le\max_{j}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\Bigr\}, \tag{11}

the distance of the bulk per cell to the range of the reference means. The paper states only that this probability “decays in t with sub-Gaussian tails”, with constants that depend on the type variances, and that computing “the precise tail bounds” requires the true composition; it prints no constant. The second statistic uses a composition \hat{\boldsymbol p}_{\cdot i} and the scale a_i:

D_{gi}=\frac{\tilde y_{gi}}{a_i}-\sum_{j=1}^{J}\hat p_{ji}\,\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}, \qquad S_M=\sum_{g\in M}\frac{D_{gi}}{\operatorname{sd}D_{gi}}, \tag{12}

with S_M its standardised sum over a gene module M. Under a consistent platform D_{gi} is centred at 0; a gene-wise ratio \tilde b_g\neq1 shifts it by (\tilde b_g-1)\sum_jp_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}. A gene is flagged when \lvert D_{gi}\rvert exceeds a threshold t_{\alpha} that a consistent gene exceeds with probability at most \alpha. The thresholds come from concentration inequalities, recalled without proof in three notes, and from five tail statements (Section 4.2.1).

Note 1: Sub-exponential variables

Vershynin’s Proposition 2.8.1 (2nd ed., p. 44) states that, for a random variable X, the following properties are equivalent, with parameters \eta_i>0 that differ by at most an absolute constant factor TODO-cite: Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press:

  • (i) Tails. \mathbb{P}\{\lvert X\rvert\ge t\}\le2\exp(-t/\eta_1) for all t\ge0.
  • (ii) Moments. (\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert^{\nu})^{1/\nu}\le\eta_2\,\nu for every moment order \nu\ge1.
  • (iii) MGF of \lvert X\rvert. \operatorname{E}\exp(\lvert X\rvert/\eta_3)\le2.
  • (iv) MGF. If \operatorname{E}X=0, (i)–(iii) are also equivalent to \operatorname{E}\exp(uX)\le\exp(\eta_4^{2}u^{2}) for all \lvert u\rvert\le1/\eta_4.

Property i implies property j with \eta_j\le\gamma'\eta_i for an absolute constant \gamma' (footnote 7). The sub-exponential norm is the smallest \eta_3 in (iii) (Definition 2.8.4, Eq. 2.25, p. 45):

\lVert X\rVert_{\psi_1}=\inf\bigl\{\eta>0:\ \operatorname{E}\exp(\lvert X\rvert/\eta)\le2\bigr\}. \tag{13}

Centring costs an absolute constant, \lVert X-\operatorname{E}X\rVert_{\psi_1}\le\gamma'\lVert X\rVert_{\psi_1} (Eq. 2.26, p. 46). Bounded variables are sub-Gaussian, and sub-Gaussian variables are sub-exponential (Remark 2.8.8, p. 46). A product of two sub-Gaussian variables is sub-exponential (Lemma 2.8.6), so sample variances and covariances, the inputs of 3.2, concentrate as Bernstein’s inequality describes, not Hoeffding’s (our remark).

NB counts. Let X follow an NB law with mean m and size \psi, \mathbb{P}(X=x)=\binom{x+\psi-1}{x}\pi^{x}(1-\pi)^{\psi} for x\in\{0,1,\dots\}, \pi=m/(m+\psi) and variance m+m^{2}/\psi (the law of Equation 3 with m=m_{gc}, \psi=\psi_g). Its moment generating function is (our derivation)

M(u) =\operatorname{E}e^{uX} =\Bigl(\frac{1-\pi}{1-\pi e^{u}}\Bigr)^{\psi}, \qquad u<-\log\pi , \tag{14}

and it is infinite for u\ge-\log\pi. Finite in an open interval around 0, it gives property (iii) for the centred NB, which is therefore sub-exponential (our derivation). It is not sub-Gaussian: a sub-Gaussian variable has a finite moment generating function at every u, and Equation 14 diverges at -\log\pi. On the log scale the tail \mathbb{P}(X\ge x) is linear in x, not quadratic. Vershynin’s list of sub-exponential laws contains the Poisson and the geometric but not the NB (Example 2.8.7, p. 46). For an integer \psi the NB is a sum of \psi geometric variables; Equation 14 covers every \psi>0.

Note 2: Hoeffding’s inequality

Let X_1,\dots,X_n be independent, and let X_\nu take its values in an interval of length A_\nu. Then, for every t>0, \mathbb{P}\{\sum_{\nu}(X_\nu-\operatorname{E}X_\nu)\ge t\}\le\exp(-2t^{2}/\sum_{\nu}A_\nu^{2}), and the same bound holds for the lower tail (Vershynin, Theorem 2.2.6, p. 30; Mohri, Rostamizadeh & Talwalkar 2012, Theorem D.1, p. 370) TODO-cite: Mohri, Rostamizadeh & Talwalkar 2012, Foundations of Machine Learning, MIT Press, Appendix D (book pp. 369-378). The variables must be bounded and independent. The bound uses the ranges, not the variances.

RNA-Sieve’s likelihood rests on “the classical CLT … as long as \operatorname{Var}(\nu_{g,k})<\infty, which is true because gene expression profiles are necessarily bounded” (PDF p. 10, Genome Res. p. 1803). A central limit theorem gives no tail bound at finite sample size; the sub-Gaussian claim follows from boundedness. With the expression of gene g in one cell in [0,A_g], Hoeffding’s inequality for the means of the n_i bulk cells and of the C_j reference cells, and a union bound, give (our derivation)

\mathbb{P}\bigl(\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t\bigr) \;\le\; 2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{n_i\,t^2}{2A_g^2}\Bigr) +2\sum_{j=1}^{J}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{C_j\,t^2}{2A_g^2}\Bigr), \tag{15}

because the expected bulk lies in the range of the expected type means (Equation 8), so \delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t requires a deviation of at least t/2 of the bulk mean or of one reference mean. Like the paper’s model, the bound treats the bulk as n_i independent cells; it is conservative. Counts have no bound A_g.

Note 3: Bernstein’s inequality

Sub-exponential form (Vershynin, Theorem 2.9.1, p. 47). Let X_1,\dots,X_n be independent, mean-zero, sub-exponential. Then, for every t\ge0,

\mathbb{P}\Bigl\{\Bigl\lvert\sum_{\nu=1}^{n}X_\nu\Bigr\rvert\ge t\Bigr\} \le 2\exp\Bigl[-\gamma\min\Bigl(\frac{t^{2}}{\sum_{\nu}\lVert X_\nu\rVert_{\psi_1}^{2}},\ \frac{t}{\max_\nu\lVert X_\nu\rVert_{\psi_1}}\Bigr)\Bigr], \tag{16}

where \gamma>0 is an absolute constant that the theorem does not give. The bound “has two tails – gaussian and exponential” (Remark 2.9.3, p. 48): Gaussian for small deviations and exponential for large ones, where a single dominant term drives the tail (Remark 2.9.4, p. 48).

Bounded form, explicit constants (Vershynin, Theorem 2.9.5, p. 49). If moreover \lvert X_\nu\rvert\le A for all \nu, then \mathbb{P}\{\lvert\sum_\nu X_\nu\rvert\ge t\}\le2\exp\bigl(-\tfrac{t^{2}/2}{\operatorname{Var}(\sum_\nu X_\nu)+At/3}\bigr). Mohri et al. state the one-sided version for the mean, with X_\nu\le A from above only (Exercise D.4, Eq. D.25, p. 378); with t equal to n times the deviation of the mean, it is the same bound. Unlike Hoeffding’s, this bound uses the variance.

Apply Equation 16 to the centred cell counts. Let L_0 be the \psi_1 norm of the centred count of gene g in one bulk cell, and L_j that of one reference cell of type j. The union bound behind Equation 15 then gives (our derivation)

\mathbb{P}\bigl(\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t\bigr) \le 2\exp\Bigl[-\gamma\,n_i\min\Bigl(\frac{t^{2}}{4L_0^{2}},\frac{t}{2L_0}\Bigr)\Bigr] +2\sum_{j=1}^{J}\exp\Bigl[-\gamma\,C_j\min\Bigl(\frac{t^{2}}{4L_j^{2}},\frac{t}{2L_j}\Bigr)\Bigr]. \tag{17}

For t\le2L each term is a Gaussian tail, the shape of Equation 15 with the range A_g replaced by the \psi_1 norm and an unknown constant; for t\ge2L it is an exponential tail, linear in t. Under NB counts the tail of Equation 11 is therefore sub-exponential in t, and the sub-Gaussian decay that RNA-Sieve states holds only for small t (our remark). A bulk cell is a mixture of types; its uncentred \psi_1 norm is at most the largest norm of the types, so L_0 is finite for NB types whatever the composition (our remark).

An explicit bound for NB cells. The constant \gamma is unknown, so Equation 17 gives the shape of the tail but no threshold. For the mean \bar X of n independent NB cells with mean m and size \psi, Markov’s inequality applied to e^{un\bar X} and the exact Equation 14 give the Cramér–Chernoff bounds (our derivation)

\mathbb{P}(\bar X-m\ge t)\le e^{-nK^{\ast}(m+t)}, \qquad \mathbb{P}(\bar X-m\le-t)\le e^{-nK^{\ast}(m-t)}, \qquad K^{\ast}(\bar x)=\sup_{u<-\log\pi}\bigl[u\bar x-\log M(u)\bigr], \tag{18}

for t>0. The supremum is attained at e^{u^{\ast}}=\bar x(m+\psi)/\{m(\bar x+\psi)\} and has the closed form (our derivation)

K^{\ast}(\bar x)=\bar x\log\frac{\bar x(m+\psi)}{m(\bar x+\psi)}+\psi\log\frac{m+\psi}{\bar x+\psi}, \qquad \bar x\ge0, \tag{19}

with 0\log0=0 and K^{\ast}(\bar x)=+\infty for \bar x<0. K^{\ast} is convex, with K^{\ast}(m)=0 and K^{\ast}(0)=\psi\log(1+m/\psi)=-\log\mathbb{P}(X=0). As \psi\to\infty, K^{\ast}(\bar x)\to\bar x\log(\bar x/m)-\bar x+m, the Poisson rate. The union bound applied to \delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g then gives, with K^{\ast}_j the rate of type j and K^{\ast}_0 that of a bulk cell,

\mathbb{P}\bigl(\delta^{\mathrm{R}}_g\ge t\bigr) \le \sum_{\pm}e^{-n_iK^{\ast}_0(\operatorname{E}\tilde y_{g}\pm t/2)} +\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{\pm}e^{-C_jK^{\ast}_j(\tilde\mu_{gj}\pm t/2)}. \tag{20}

For the bulk mixture, K^{\ast}_0 has no closed form and is a one-dimensional numerical maximisation. Like the precise tail bounds RNA-Sieve mentions, Equation 20 needs the true parameters (composition, means and sizes).

4.2.1 Five tail statements for the discrepancy

The range distance Equation 11 does not use the composition and loses power through the union bound. The discrepancy Equation 12 uses it, and its law has an exact cumulant generating function under NB counts. The five statements below are exactly those implemented in scripts/figures/fig_03_1_tail_bounds.R; they are ordered by increasing complexity and labelled T1 to T5 as in the figures. They hold under four assumptions, for one gene g and one bulk sample i (index i dropped, D=D_{gi}).

  • (A1) Cells. Counts of different cells are independent. A cell of type j has an NB count with mean \tilde\mu_{gj} and size \psi_g, \pi_{gj}=\tilde\mu_{gj}/(\tilde\mu_{gj}+\psi_g) (Equation 14).
  • (A2) Composition. The bulk contains exactly m_{j}=p_jn cells of type j (fixed integers).
  • (A3) Platforms. Bulk and reference cells of type j have the same law: a_i=1, no gene-wise platform ratio, no extra overdispersion. Bulk and reference are independent.
  • (A4) Known parameters. \boldsymbol p, \tilde\mu_{g\cdot} and \psi_g are known, so \hat p_j=p_j in Equation 12. No statement below accounts for estimated parameters (Section 4.2.3).

Under (A1)–(A4), D=\tilde y_{g}-\sum_jp_j\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj} is a sum of n independent bulk terms and C_j independent reference terms per type, with

\operatorname{E}D=0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}D=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{p_j\sigma_{gj}^2}{n}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{p_j^2\sigma_{gj}^2}{C_j}, \tag{21}

and cumulant generating function

K_D(u)=\log\operatorname{E}e^{uD} =\sum_{j=1}^{J}m_{j}K_{gj}\Bigl(\frac{u}{n}\Bigr) +\sum_{j=1}^{J}C_jK_{gj}\Bigl(-\frac{u\,p_j}{C_j}\Bigr), \qquad K_{gj}(u)=-\psi_g\log\Bigl(1-\frac{\tilde\mu_{gj}}{\psi_g}\bigl(e^{u}-1\bigr)\Bigr), \tag{22}

K_{gj} the per-cell cumulant generating function of type j (Equation 14), defined for u_-<u<u_+ with u_+=n\min_j(-\log\pi_{gj}) and u_-=\max_jC_j\log\pi_{gj}/p_j<0. K_D is convex with K_D(0)=K_D'(0)=0. Its Legendre transforms

K_D^{+}(t)=\sup_{0<u<u_+}\bigl[ut-K_D(u)\bigr], \qquad K_D^{-}(t)=\sup_{u_-<u<0}\bigl[-ut-K_D(u)\bigr], \qquad t>0, \tag{23}

are computed at the root of K_D'(u)=\pm t. The threshold t_{0.01} of a statement is the smallest t at which its tail probability, or its bound, equals \alpha/2=0.01; for a Chernoff bound this means K_D^{\pm}(t_{0.01})=\log100. The reference means are averages over few cells, so the reference term dominates the third cumulant of D and D is left-skewed in the simulation (skewness -0.08 and -0.06): its lower tail is the heavier one.

Modules. For a module M of \lvert M\rvert genes, two further assumptions describe the dependence between genes. Let \mathcal{H}=(M,\mathcal{E}) be a gene graph with maximal degree d_{\max} and mean degree \bar d=2\lvert\mathcal{E}\rvert/\lvert M\rvert.

  • (A5) Within-cell correlation. In one cell of any type, the counts of genes g and h have correlation \varrho when (g,h)\in\mathcal{E} and 0 otherwise; different cells are independent.
  • (A6) Dependency graph. Sets of genes with no edge between them have independent counts in every cell. Genes of an independent set of \mathcal{H} are then mutually independent.

With c_{ghj}=\varrho\,\sigma_{gj}\sigma_{hj} on an edge, and since bulk and reference are independent,

\operatorname{Cov}(D_g,D_h)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{p_j\,c_{ghj}}{n}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{p_j^2\,c_{ghj}}{C_j}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}S_M=\lvert M\rvert+2\sum_{(g,h)\in\mathcal{E}}\operatorname{Corr}(D_g,D_h), \tag{24}

with S_M=\sum_{g\in M}Z_g, Z_g=D_g/\operatorname{sd}D_g and \operatorname{Corr}(D_g,D_h)\le\varrho by Cauchy–Schwarz. In the simulation (\lvert M\rvert=20 genes, 30 edges, d_{\max}=6, \bar d=3, \varrho=0.3), \operatorname{Var}S_M=37.2 against 20 for independent genes. The statements below were written for graphs with d_{\max}\le10 and \bar d\le3.

Theorem 1 (T1, Lindeberg–Feller Gaussian approximation)

Under (A1)–(A4), D is a sum of independent terms that are identically distributed within each of 2J groups, with finite variances, and a term of type j carries at most a fraction 1/m_j (bulk) or 1/C_j (reference) of \operatorname{Var}D. As every m_j and every C_j grow with \boldsymbol p fixed, Lindeberg’s condition holds and D/\operatorname{sd}D converges in law to \mathcal{N}(0,1). The approximation used is

\mathbb{P}(D\ge t)\approx1-\Phi\Bigl(\frac{t}{\operatorname{sd}D}\Bigr), \qquad \mathbb{P}(D\le-t)\approx\Phi\Bigl(-\frac{t}{\operatorname{sd}D}\Bigr), \qquad t_{0.01}=z_{0.99}\operatorname{sd}D, \tag{25}

with z_{0.99}=2.326 and \operatorname{sd}D from Equation 21. It is an approximation, not a bound: no error term is evaluated, and it is symmetric in the two tails.

RNA-Sieve’s likelihood rests on this Gaussian approximation (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021, Eqs 5, 7, 9). The Lindeberg argument above is ours and is not machine-checked.

Corollary 1 (T1-log, log-normal approximation of the ratio)

Let R=\tilde y_{g}\big/\sum_jp_j\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj} and \bar\mu_g=\sum_jp_j\tilde\mu_{gj}, with \tilde y_g>0. To first order (delta method), \log R\approx D/\bar\mu_g and \operatorname{Var}\log R\approx\operatorname{Var}D/\bar\mu_g^{2}. Taking \log R Gaussian and centred at 0, and replacing the random denominator by \bar\mu_g, gives the thresholds

t_{0.01}^{+}=\bar\mu_g\bigl(e^{z_{0.99}\operatorname{sd}D/\bar\mu_g}-1\bigr), \qquad t_{0.01}^{-}=\bar\mu_g\bigl(1-e^{-z_{0.99}\operatorname{sd}D/\bar\mu_g}\bigr). \tag{26}

It is an approximation in three steps (delta method, normality of \log R without the -\operatorname{Var}\log R/2 shift, fixed denominator), not a bound.

The log-ratio form matches RNA-Sieve’s bulk-to-reference ratio, one of its four MAD statistics; RNA-Sieve itself prints no log-scale central limit theorem. Gibrat’s law does not apply: it gives a log-normal limit for a product of many independent factors, and a bulk is a sum of cells. The log-normal shape here comes only from the delta method. In the simulation the variance step is accurate (Monte Carlo \operatorname{sd}\log R=0.0601 against 0.0600 from the formula for the low-expression gene), but the shape is not: the approximation implies a right-skewed ratio, whereas D is left-skewed, so T1-log errs on the anti-conservative side in the lower tail.

Theorem 2 (T2, Gaussian approximation on a dependency graph)

Under (A1)–(A6), \mathcal{H} is a dependency graph for (Z_g)_{g\in M}, and the approximation used is

\mathbb{P}(S_M\ge t)\approx1-\Phi\Bigl(\frac{t}{\sigma_S}\Bigr), \qquad \mathbb{P}(S_M\le-t)\approx\Phi\Bigl(-\frac{t}{\sigma_S}\Bigr), \tag{27}

with \sigma_S^2=\operatorname{Var}S_M of Equation 24.

Baldi & Rinott (1989) and Chen & Shao (2004, Theorem 2.7) bound the error of this normal approximation in terms of the maximal degree and of moments above the second. That error bound is not evaluated here.

TODO-cite: Baldi & Rinott 1989, On normal approximations of distributions in terms of dependency graphs, Ann. Probab. 17(4) TODO-cite: Chen & Shao 2004, Normal approximation under local dependence, Ann. Probab. 32(3A):1985-2028, doi:10.1214/009117904000000450 The Gaussian approximation with \operatorname{Var}S_M=\lvert M\rvert, which ignores the edges, is T1 for the module. The bound of Chen & Shao is the result that MEAD uses for its central limit theorem across genes (Section 8).

Theorem 3 (T3, Chernoff bound with Poisson cumulant generating functions)

Replace each K_{gj} in Equation 22 by the Poisson cumulant generating function \tilde\mu_{gj}(e^{u}-1):

K^{\mathrm{Pois}}_D(u)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}m_{j}\tilde\mu_{gj}\bigl(e^{u/n}-1\bigr) +\sum_{j=1}^{J}C_j\tilde\mu_{gj}\bigl(e^{-up_j/C_j}-1\bigr), \qquad u\in\mathbb{R}. \tag{28}

If the counts are Poisson (\psi_g=\infty) and (A1)–(A4) hold, then for t>0, with the transforms Equation 23 of K^{\mathrm{Pois}}_D, \mathbb{P}(D\ge t)\le\exp\{-K^{\mathrm{Pois},+}_D(t)\} and \mathbb{P}(D\le-t)\le\exp\{-K^{\mathrm{Pois},-}_D(t)\}. For a single sum of n cells with mean m (no reference term), the rate has the closed form n\{\bar x\log(\bar x/m)-\bar x+m\} at \bar x=m\pm t. Under NB counts the statement is not a bound: the Poisson model understates the per-cell variance by the factor 1+\tilde\mu_{gj}/\psi_g.

For the module, T3 adds the transforms over genes as if they were independent, with the NB standard deviations in Z_g; it is then misspecified twice (Poisson margins, independence).

Theorem 4 (T4, Chernoff bound with the exact NB cumulant generating function)

Under (A1)–(A4), for every t>0 and every n, C_j,

\mathbb{P}(D\ge t)\le\exp\bigl\{-K_D^{+}(t)\bigr\}, \qquad \mathbb{P}(D\le-t)\le\exp\bigl\{-K_D^{-}(t)\bigr\}, \tag{29}

with K_D^{\pm} the transforms Equation 23 of the exact Equation 22. The bound follows from Markov’s inequality applied to e^{uD}; its prefactor is 1 and it has no unknown constant, unlike Equation 16 and Equation 17.

With J=1 and no reference noise (C_1=\infty), T4 reduces to Equation 18 with n bulk cells. For the module, T4 sums the cumulant generating functions K_{D_g}(u/\operatorname{sd}D_g) over genes: it is a finite-sample bound if the genes are independent, and it is not under (A5) with \varrho>0.

Theorem 5 (T5, NB Chernoff bound after a proper colouring, after Janson)

Under (A1)–(A4) for every gene and (A6), let \mathcal{M}_1,\dots,\mathcal{M}_{\chi_G} be a proper colouring of \mathcal{H}, that is a partition of M into \chi_G classes with no edge inside a class. One exists with

\chi_G\le\bar\chi_G=\min\Bigl(d_{\max}+1,\ \frac{1+\sqrt{8\lvert\mathcal{E}\rvert+1}}{2}\Bigr). \tag{30}

By convexity of the exponential and independence within each class, for every u in the domain,

\operatorname{E}e^{uS_M} \le\frac{1}{\chi_G}\sum_{c=1}^{\chi_G}\prod_{g\in\mathcal{M}_c}\operatorname{E}e^{\chi_GuZ_g} =\exp\bar K_S(u), \qquad \bar K_S(u)=\log\Bigl(\frac{1}{\chi_G}\sum_{c=1}^{\chi_G}\exp\sum_{g\in\mathcal{M}_c}K_{D_g}\Bigl(\frac{\chi_Gu}{\operatorname{sd}D_g}\Bigr)\Bigr), \tag{31}

and therefore, for t>0,

\mathbb{P}(S_M\ge t)\le\inf_{u>0}\exp\{-ut+\bar K_S(u)\}, \qquad \mathbb{P}(S_M\le-t)\le\inf_{u<0}\exp\{ut+\bar K_S(u)\}, \tag{32}

with \chi_Gu/\operatorname{sd}D_g inside the domain of every K_{D_g}. The bound holds for any dependence between colour classes, does not use \varrho, and has no unknown constant.

TODO-cite: Janson 2004, Large deviations for sums of partly dependent random variables, Random Struct. Algorithms 24(3), doi:10.1002/rsa.20008 Both degree conditions enter through \chi_G: the maximal degree through d_{\max}+1, the number of edges, hence the mean degree, through the second term of Equation 30. The greedy colouring with vertices in decreasing degree order (Welsh & Powell 1967) TODO-cite: Welsh & Powell 1967, An upper bound for the chromatic number of a graph, Comput. J. 10(1) attains both bounds (our remark); in the simulation it uses \chi_G=3 classes of 8, 7 and 5 genes, against \bar\chi_G=7. The price of the colouring is the factor \chi_G inside the argument: near u=0, \bar K_S(u)\approx \chi_G\lvert M\rvert u^{2}/2, an effective variance of 60 against \operatorname{Var}S_M=37.2. Janson (2004) states the bound for fractional covers by independent sets with weights; the equal-weight proper colouring is the special case used here (this remark is not checked against the paper). The dependent Bernstein inequality of Zhang & Li, used by DECALS, has a constant equal to \bar\chi_G and an unknown absolute constant in the exponent (Equation 39, Section 8).

4.2.2 Comparing the statements

Figure 7 and Figure 8 compare the statements with Monte Carlo tails for a bulk of n=10^4 cells with \boldsymbol p=(0.6,0.3,0.1), a reference with C_j=2000,300,30 cells and NB counts with \psi_g=2, all parameters known. Table 4 reads the thresholds at the common level \alpha/2=0.01 per side.

Read from Table 4:

  • Most conservative. Per gene, T4 has the largest threshold in all four panels, 1.29 to 1.33 times the Monte Carlo one. Per module, T5 has the largest, 1.70 to 1.72 times.
  • Least conservative. T3 has the smallest threshold for the high-expression gene (a quarter of the Monte Carlo one) and for the module. For the low-expression gene, whose variance factor 1+\tilde\mu_{gj}/\psi_g is at most 1.3, T3 is the second most conservative statement.
  • Under-coverage. A threshold below the Monte Carlo interval rejects more than 1 % of consistent genes in that tail. This happens for T1 and T1-log in the lower tail of both genes, for T3 in both tails of the high-expression gene, for T1, T3 and T4 in both tails of the module, and for T2 in the lower tail of the module (0.8 % below Monte Carlo). Only the two finite-sample bounds whose assumptions hold, T4 for one gene and T5 for a module, never under-cover.
  • Far tail. In a separate run with the same seed, the T4 to Monte Carlo ratio falls from 1.29–1.33 at 0.01 to 1.11–1.14 at 10^{-5}, and the lower-tail T1 ratio from 0.98 to 0.94–0.95: the Gaussian under-coverage grows further out.

Multiplicity. The level \alpha/2=0.01 per side is per gene. Over about 3,000 genes a correctly calibrated filter flags about 60 consistent genes at this level. A Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg correction moves the threshold into the far tail, where the Gaussian statements under-cover more and the Chernoff bounds come closer to the truth.

Note 4: Link with non-parametric quantile regression

Each statement bounds or approximates the (1-\alpha/2) quantile of \lvert D_g\rvert under a count model, gene by gene. Quantile regression (Koenker & Bassett 1978) TODO-cite: Koenker & Bassett 1978, Regression quantiles, Econometrica 46(1):33-50, doi:10.2307/1913643 estimates the conditional quantile Q_{1-\alpha/2}(\tilde y_{gi}\mid\hat y_{gi}) of the bulk given the fitted bulk \hat y_{gi}=\sum_j\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}, pooled across genes and without a count model. Conformalised quantile regression (Romano, Patterson & Candès 2019) TODO-cite: Romano, Patterson & Candès 2019, Conformalized quantile regression, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32, arXiv:1905.03222 adds a finite-sample coverage guarantee under exchangeability of the genes. Genes differ in mean and are correlated, so that guarantee is marginal over genes, not per gene. The two approaches answer the same question with different assumptions: the bounds need a correct model and known parameters, the band needs exchangeable genes. The reproducibility book compares the flags of all five statements with such a band on the Suppinger data.

4.2.3 Plug-in parameters

Assumption (A4) never holds in practice. The application plugs in the following estimates.

  • Composition. \hat{\boldsymbol p}_{\cdot i} comes from deMixSC-style iterated weighted NNLS of \tilde y_{gi} on the reference means, with weights w_{gi}^{-1}=\hat y_{gi}^{2}+(\tilde y_{gi}-\hat y_{gi})^{2}+c_w, c_w=2 (Guo et al. 2023, Eq. 4, PDF p. 12). deMixSC also splits the genes into a low-discrepancy set and a high-discrepancy set \mathcal{G}_2 whose residuals are down-weighted. \mathcal{G}_2 is empty here: deMixSC builds it from a benchmark of bulk and single-nucleus data from the same aliquots (PDF p. 11), which a one-specimen reference lacks.
  • Scale. a_i is the sum of the NNLS coefficients, which estimate a_ip_{ji}; \hat{\boldsymbol p}_{\cdot i} is the normalised coefficient vector.
  • Dispersion. \psi_g comes from the reference fit of tier (ii), and the extra overdispersion between platforms is fixed at 1 (none).

With these plug-ins every statement is approximate, including T4 and T5: they are exact only at the true parameters. Because \hat{\boldsymbol p}_{\cdot i} is fitted to the same bulk, the fitted discrepancies are expected to be smaller than under the true composition, so the plug-in thresholds should err on the conservative side for genes that do not drive the fit (our remark, not checked by simulation).

5 Tier (iv): down-weighting by the model

Filters remove genes; a weighted likelihood keeps them and lets their variance decide their influence. The reviewed methods sit on a ladder of noise models (Table 5; full ladder in 5.1).

Two observations follow.

  • DECALS computes its point estimate by constrained ordinary least squares and uses the covariance only for inference, because a GLS fit with an estimated covariance per sample was biased in their experiments (Cai et al. 2024, 6). The same risk applies to any feasible GLS whose covariance is estimated on few cells; shrinkage of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} addresses it (3.2).
  • MEAD notes that removing genes brings no efficiency gain unless their noise levels differ (Xie et al. 2026, 17). Once the covariance is in the model, hard filtering is needed only for genes outside the model’s support: the presence gate (Section 2.2) and, when a matched bulk exists, the cross-platform outliers of tier
    1. (Section 4).

6 Selection effect on the covariance

Selecting genes changes the covariance that is then estimated on them.

  • Small within-type variance by construction. A ratio such as \mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{B},g}/\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{W},g} of Equation 5 rewards a small within-type part. ReDeconv goes further and keeps the genes with the smallest coefficient of variation (Lu et al. 2025, 14); MuSiC’s tree-guided stage keeps genes with small intra-cluster variance (Wang et al. 2019, 8). A panel chosen this way removes much of the within-type covariance that DeCovarT models, and the estimated \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} on that panel is close to diagonal for that reason, not because genes are conditionally independent (3.2).
  • Weak marginal effects hide interactions. Genes with weak marginal effects are dropped by every univariate screen, and gene pairs whose signal lies in their covariance, not in their means, are then never examined. Covariance-aware criteria (Section 7.4.4,
    1. can recover them only from a shortlist that still contains them.

Screening on marginal effects first is the practice that the design of experiments justifies with three principles (Wu & Hamada 2021, §4.6) TODO-cite: Wu & Hamada 2021, Experiments: Planning, Analysis, and Optimization, 3rd ed., Wiley, Section 4.6 (no DOI). Effect sparsity says that few effects are active (Box & Meyer 1986) TODO-cite: Box & Meyer 1986, An analysis for unreplicated fractional factorials, Technometrics 28(1), doi:10.1080/00401706.1986.10488093. Effect hierarchy says that main effects are more likely to be active than two-factor interactions, and these more than higher-order ones. Effect heredity says that an interaction is active only if one (weak heredity) or both (strong heredity) of its parent main effects are active; it guides the analysis of designs with complex aliasing (Hamada & Wu 1992) and the priors of Bayesian variable selection with related predictors (Chipman 1996) TODO-cite: Hamada & Wu 1992, Analysis of designed experiments with complex aliasing, J. Qual. Technol. 24(3), doi:10.1080/00224065.1992.11979383 TODO-cite: Chipman 1996, Bayesian variable selection with related predictors, Can. J. Stat. 24(1), doi:10.2307/3315687. The marginality principle of linear models, that a model with an interaction should contain the main effects it involves, is the model-building counterpart (Nelder 1977) TODO-cite: Nelder 1977, A reformulation of linear models, J. R. Stat. Soc. A 140(1), doi:10.2307/2344517.

  • Empirical support. The principles were checked on published experiments: a meta-analysis of 113 factorial data sets (Li, Sudarsanam & Frey 2006) and a meta-analysis of response-surface experiments (Ockuly et al. 2017) TODO-cite: Li, Sudarsanam & Frey 2006, Regularities in data from factorial experiments, Complexity 11(5), doi:10.1002/cplx.20123 TODO-cite: Ockuly et al. 2017, Response surface experiments: a meta-analysis, Chemometr. Intell. Lab. Syst. 164, doi:10.1016/j.chemolab.2017.03.009. Their estimated frequencies are not quoted here; they are to be read from the papers.
  • Methods built on heredity. The lasso for hierarchical interactions enforces heredity as a constraint (Bien, Taylor & Tibshirani 2013), and interaction screening for ultrahigh-dimensional data searches interactions among the variables kept by a marginal screen (Hao & Zhang 2014) TODO-cite: Bien, Taylor & Tibshirani 2013, A lasso for hierarchical interactions, Ann. Stat. 41(3), doi:10.1214/13-AOS1096 TODO-cite: Hao & Zhang 2014, Interaction screening for ultrahigh-dimensional data, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 109, doi:10.1080/01621459.2014.881741.
  • Counter-examples. Sure independence screening misses variables that are marginally uncorrelated with the response but jointly important, which motivated its iterated version (Fan & Lv 2008). Genetic models can show epistasis with no main effect at all (Culverhouse et al. 2002). Differential networking describes genes whose connections change between conditions while their expression level does not (de la Fuente 2010) TODO-cite: Fan & Lv 2008, Sure independence screening for ultrahigh dimensional feature space, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 70(5), doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00674.x TODO-cite: Culverhouse, Suarez, Lin & Reich 2002, A perspective on epistasis: limits of models displaying no main effect, Am. J. Hum. Genet. 70(2), doi:10.1086/338759 TODO-cite: de la Fuente 2010, From ‘differential expression’ to ‘differential networking’, Trends Genet. 26(7), doi:10.1016/j.tig.2010.05.001.

Heredity is an empirical regularity, a default assumption rather than a theorem, and it fails precisely for covariance-only signal. A gene pair whose types differ only in their correlation has no parent main effect, so a marginal screen followed by a heredity-constrained search cannot find it.

A practical check is to compare the distribution of v_{gj}, and of the off-diagonal entries of \boldsymbol{V}_j, between the selected panel and the genes that pass the presence gate.

7 Perspectives

7.1 Cross-sample consistency

Cross-sample consistency compares a gene across specimens, the subjects or donors of the reference. It needs at least two specimens, so a one-specimen reference cannot assess it.

  • Cross-subject variance (MuSiC). MuSiC’s cross-subject consistency guards against the choice of subjects (Wang et al. 2019, 2). Its weights down-weight genes with a large cross-subject variance (Eq. 10, p. 7), and an optional gene- and subject-specific intercept absorbs subject effects (p. 7). With R\ge2 donors this variance is the between-donor covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j} of 2.1.
  • Pseudo-bulk differential expression. DESeq2, edgeR or limma–voom on donor-level pseudo-bulks test a population contrast with donors as replicates (Love et al. 2014; Crowell et al. 2020). Appendix S6 uses them only for multi-donor references (S6).

Two cell lines profiled in one experiment are the closest available analogue of two specimens; the reproducibility book has a sensitivity analysis on the two cell lines at 48 h.

7.2 Cross-technology references

Two single-cell references of the same tissue from different technologies (droplet against plate-based, single-cell against single-nucleus) measure the same types with different gene-wise capture efficiencies b_g. Their comparison needs no composition: the type means can be compared type by type, so the range and discrepancy statistics of Section 4.2 reduce to differences \hat{\tilde\mu}^{(1)}_{gj}-\hat{\tilde\mu}^{(2)}_{gj}, with both sides estimated from cells. Genes whose ratio \hat{\tilde\mu}^{(1)}_{gj}/\hat{\tilde\mu}^{(2)}_{gj} varies across types are inconsistent between technologies whatever the scale; a ratio constant across types is a gene-wise capture ratio, which MEAD’s model absorbs. This needs a common annotation of the types in both references.

7.3 Dependent cells in a tissue

Assumption (A1) treats the cells of one bulk as independent. In a tissue, neighbouring cells share a microenvironment, so the counts of a gene in two neighbouring cells can be correlated. A neighbourhood graph on the cells of a bulk, gene by gene, would then play the role of the gene graph \mathcal{H} of Section 4.2.1. The colouring argument of Theorem 5 applies unchanged to the sum over cells: with the cells coloured into \chi_G classes of mutually independent cells, the moment generating function of the bulk total is bounded by the average over classes of products of per-cell terms evaluated at \chi_Gu. The dependency-graph central limit theorem of Theorem 2 applies in the same way. Spatial transcriptomics would supply the graph; its maximal degree sets \chi_G.

7.4 Covariance-driven (post hoc) feature selection

The gate of tier (ii) runs before any covariance is estimated, gene by gene, and uses no per-type characteristic beyond the labels. The criteria below treat the panel \mathcal{G} as a subset-selection problem on the full J-column signature and use the within-type covariance or precision matrices, so they can run only after \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} (or \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_j) has been estimated on a shortlist (3.2, 3.3). The likelihood of DeCovarT depends on \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p} and on the covariance mixture, so this is the geometry of the model; it is also why the stage is post hoc.

Warning 2: Circularity

A panel optimised for DeCovarT’s own information makes DeCovarT’s later performance on that panel uninterpretable: a gain can come from the panel or from the model. A comparison with other methods must use a panel chosen without the model, such as the tier (ii) gate, or report both panels, and every covariance-driven step must be repeated inside the training folds (S6).

7.4.1 The ANOVA ratio is a screen, not the objective

Take J=2, one gene, the population model of DeCovarT (1.2) and equal within-type variances \sigma_g^2. Then y_g\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(p\mu_{g1}+(1-p)\mu_{g2},\,\sigma_g^2 s(p)\bigr) with s(p)=p^2+(1-p)^2, and the Fisher information for p is

I_g(p) = \frac{\Delta_g^{2}}{s(p)} + \frac12\Bigl(\frac{s'(p)}{s(p)}\Bigr)^{2}, \qquad \Delta_g=\frac{\mu_{g1}-\mu_{g2}}{\sigma_g}. \tag{33}

The second term is the same for every gene, so I_g(p) is affine in \Delta_g^2 with a positive slope. Computed on the scale of the model, the one-way ANOVA ratio F_g=\{\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{B},g}/(J-1)\}/\{\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{W},g}/(C-J)\} estimates \Delta_g^2: F_g is non-central F_{1,C-2} with non-centrality \tilde C\Delta_g^{2}, \tilde C=C_1C_2/C, so \operatorname{E}F_g\approx1+\tilde C\Delta_g^2 (exactly, a factor \nu/(\nu-2) with \nu=C-2 multiplies this). Ranking genes by F_g therefore ranks them by I_g(p) at every p, and with independent genes, whose informations add, the top-ranked genes by F_g maximise the total information \sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}I_g(p). The univariate ratio is a screen; the objective for a panel is the Fisher information for \boldsymbol{p} of the whole panel. The ratio ignores:

  • redundancy and collinearity. Two genes that separate the same pair of types add little information together, and concatenated one-versus-rest lists inflate the condition number of \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}} (1);
  • the covariance DeCovarT models. With \sigma_{g1}\ne\sigma_{g2} the information depends on p through p^2\sigma_{g1}^2+(1-p)^2\sigma_{g2}^2, and with correlated genes the informations add only at isolated values of the correlation;
  • the count mean–variance relation, unless the ratio is computed on residuals of a model with the right variance function (Section 3.2).

7.4.2 Multivariate tests

A multivariate test would replace the G gene-wise nulls by one null on the vector \boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}. Two routes are often confused.

  • Gene-wise GEE is still gene-wise. GEE extends the quasi-score to a vector of correlated observations, with a working covariance (Liang & Zeger 1986) TODO-cite: Liang & Zeger 1986, Longitudinal data analysis using generalized linear models, Biometrika 73:13-22, doi:10.1093/biomet/73.1.13. Fitted once per gene, it still returns G p-values and still needs FDR control: correlation-aware inference does not remove multiplicity.
  • A joint test needs \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j. A Hotelling or MANOVA test of equal type means on the panel uses the within-type covariance, which is high-dimensional when C_j is not much larger than |\mathcal{G}|, as for rare types (3.2). With a regularised \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} such a test is possible on a shortlist, but its calibration is open. PERMANOVA (Section 3.2.1) avoids the inverse covariance by permuting a sum of squared distances, and a module-level version of the label permutation is a candidate.
7.4.2.1 Variance-weighted condition number

With gene-wise uncertainties \tau_g^2 (biological, sampling and optional reference-to-bulk discrepancy), standardise the rows and evaluate the conditioning in the (J-1)-dimensional contrast space induced by \sum_jp_j=1:

\kappa_2\bigl(\boldsymbol{T}_{\mathcal{G}}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}\boldsymbol{K}\bigr), \qquad \boldsymbol{T}_{\mathcal{G}}=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_g^2)_{g\in\mathcal{G}}, \tag{34}

where the J\times(J-1) matrix \boldsymbol{K} has orthonormal columns orthogonal to \mathbf{1}. Unweighted \kappa_2 can favour quiet but biased genes. Equation 34 is the square root of the condition number of the information of Section 7.4.4 with a diagonal covariance, so it still misses the covariance-only regime in which DeCovarT identifies types whose means agree (1.2).

7.4.3 Spectral entropy of a covariance (Unico)

Unico quantifies “the amount of signal coming from the covariance structure of a given gene” by the von Neumann entropy of the normalised J\times J matrix of correlations between cell types of that gene [Chen et al. (2025), pp. 19–20; review in 5.1]. The covariance is taken across samples of the cell-type-specific levels of the gene. The paper prints no formula. Let \boldsymbol{R}_g be that correlation matrix, with eigenvalues \lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_J. A von Neumann entropy needs a matrix of unit trace, and \operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R}_g=J, so we read the definition as (our reading)

H^{\mathrm{vN}}_g =-\sum_{h=1}^{J}\tilde\lambda_h\log\tilde\lambda_h =\log J-\frac1J\sum_{h=1}^{J}\lambda_h\log\lambda_h, \qquad \tilde\lambda_h=\frac{\lambda_h}{\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R}_g}=\frac{\lambda_h}{J}, \tag{35}

with 0\log0=0. The superscript separates it from the specificity entropy H_g of Equation 1. The \tilde\lambda_h form a probability vector, so 0\le H^{\mathrm{vN}}_g\le\log J. The maximum \log J is reached if and only if every \lambda_h=1, that is \boldsymbol{R}_g=\boldsymbol{I}. The minimum 0 is reached if and only if \boldsymbol{R}_g has rank one, that is all cross-type correlations equal \pm1. The paper scales the values “to the range [0,1]” because the entropy is bounded by a number that depends on the number of cell types (p. 20); dividing by \log J does this.

Unico states that “High entropy corresponds to cases where no substantial cell-type covariance structure exists, and low entropy indicates strong positive or negative correlations between cell types” (p. 20). A bound makes this precise (our remark). The Shannon entropy is at least the Rényi entropy of order 2, -\log\sum_h\tilde\lambda_h^{2}, and \sum_h\tilde\lambda_h^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{R}_g^{2})/J^{2}. With \overline{\rho^{2}}_g the mean squared off-diagonal correlation,

H^{\mathrm{vN}}_g\;\ge\;\log\frac{J}{1+(J-1)\,\overline{\rho^{2}}_g}. \tag{36}

Small correlations force a high entropy. A low entropy therefore requires large correlations on average.

How Unico uses it. The entropy stratifies genes for evaluation; it does not filter them. “Throughout our evaluation of the deconvolution results, we grouped genes into high- and low-entropy groups”, with the split at the median (p. 20). Fig. 1b shows the normalised entropy over “the top 10,000 most highly expressed genes in scRNA-seq from PBMC” (p. 2). On PBMC pseudo-bulks “the improvement of Unico is more pronounced in genes that exhibit strong cell-type covariance structure (low-entropy genes; average correlation improvement of 20.0%) compared to high-entropy genes (average improvement of 14.9%)” (p. 6). Unico keeps every gene; its benchmark gene sets are random or chosen by variance (pp. 5, 7, 19). Reading the entropy as a gene filter would go beyond the paper.

The analogue for DeCovarT. DeCovarT treats the cells of different types as independent, so the J\times J cross-type correlation of a gene is \boldsymbol{I}. Its entropy is the maximum \log J for every gene, and the criterion carries no information there. Unico’s cross-type covariance is a between-sample quantity: it is closest to the between-donor covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j} of 2.1, extended across types (our remark). The covariance DeCovarT does model is the within-type covariance across genes. The analogue is then the entropy Equation 35 of the |\mathcal{G}|\times|\mathcal{G}| within-type correlation \boldsymbol{R}_j of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} restricted to the panel, with J replaced by |\mathcal{G}| (our remark). Its exponential \exp H^{\mathrm{vN}}(\boldsymbol{R}_j) is the effective rank of \boldsymbol{R}_j TODO-cite: Roy & Vetterli 2007, The effective rank: a measure of effective dimensionality, EUSIPCO 2007; no key in the bibs: it equals |\mathcal{G}| for independent genes and 1 for a single module of perfectly correlated genes. A low entropy means a few strong shared modules, hence few effective directions in type j.

  • Against \kappa_2. The condition number of 1 uses the two extreme singular values of the mean matrix. The entropy uses the whole spectrum of a correlation matrix. Applied to \boldsymbol{R}_j, \kappa_2 flags one near-null direction, and the entropy measures how evenly the variance spreads over all directions (our remark).
  • Against D-optimality. \log\det\boldsymbol{R}_j=\sum_h\log\lambda_h is also a function of the whole spectrum. With the trace fixed at |\mathcal{G}|, both \log\det and the entropy are largest at \boldsymbol{R}_j=\boldsymbol{I} and decrease as the spectrum spreads (our remark). This does not make a low entropy bad for DeCovarT. The criteria of Section 7.4.4 score the information for \boldsymbol{p}, not \boldsymbol{R}_j, and in the example of Figure 9 a correlation of 0.8 raises \det I. What separates types is the difference between \boldsymbol{R}_j and \boldsymbol{R}_\ell, which the overlap \bar\varpi of 2 measures; a low entropy in each type is not enough.

The entropy uses no deconvolution fit, so the circularity of Warning 2 does not apply to it (our remark). It still needs \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} on a shortlist, so it is post hoc like the other criteria of this section.

7.4.4 Fisher information for \boldsymbol{p}: D-, E- and A-optimality

For a panel \mathcal{G}, restrict the rows of \boldsymbol{\mu} and the rows and columns of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j to \mathcal{G} and compute I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p}) from 1.2, Eq. for I(\boldsymbol{p}), in J-1 free coordinates \boldsymbol\theta with \boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{p}_0+\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol\theta.

For J=2 the information is a scalar. Under the single-cell model with a common within-type covariance it is n_i\boldsymbol\Delta^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W^{-1}\boldsymbol\Delta, \boldsymbol\Delta=\boldsymbol\mu_{\cdot1}-\boldsymbol\mu_{\cdot2}, the squared Mahalanobis distance between the two type means, as in the CardamomOT comparison note (section “DeCovarT”); every criterion below then ranks panels by that distance. From J=3 on, I_{\mathcal{G}} is a matrix and the criteria differ.
