Because \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}) depends on \boldsymbol{p}, a panel is scored over a composition grid \mathcal{P}\subset\Delta^{J-1} (balanced, rare-type, sparse and near-collinear compositions), and the classical criteria (Atkinson and Donev 1992; Pukelsheim 2006) become

\max_{\mathcal{G}}\min_{\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathcal{P}} \log\det I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p}) \ \text{(robust D)}, \qquad \max_{\mathcal{G}}\min_{\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathcal{P}} \lambda_{\min}\bigl(I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr) \ \text{(E)}, \qquad \min_{\mathcal{G}}\max_{\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathcal{P}} \operatorname{tr}I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1} \ \text{(A)}. \tag{37}

D-optimality shrinks the volume of the confidence ellipsoid for \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} and can leave one weak contrast; E-optimality shortens its longest axis, the worst contrast; A-optimality minimises the average variance.

The D-ranking does not depend on the basis \boldsymbol{K}, since \det I_{\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{B}}=(\det\boldsymbol{B})^2\det I_{\boldsymbol{K}}. The E- and A-rankings do: they are basis-free only when computed on \operatorname{Cov}\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}=\boldsymbol{K}I_{\boldsymbol{K}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{K}^{\top}, which amounts to an orthonormal \boldsymbol{K}. In the raw coordinates (p_1,p_2), which drop the last type, the E-ranking of two panels can reverse.

Common covariance. With \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W for every type, the covariance mixture \sum_jp_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W does not depend on \boldsymbol{p} and

I_{\mathcal{G}} = n_i\,\boldsymbol{K}^{\top}\boldsymbol{M}_{\mathcal{G}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W^{-1}\boldsymbol{M}_{\mathcal{G}}\boldsymbol{K}, \tag{38}

with \boldsymbol{M}_{\mathcal{G}} the |\mathcal{G}|\times J matrix of type means. If \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_W=\boldsymbol{I}, I_{\mathcal{G}}=n_i\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A} with \boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{M}_{\mathcal{G}}\boldsymbol{K}: D-optimality maximises the squared Gram volume of the contrasted mean columns, and \kappa_2(I_{\mathcal{G}})=\kappa_2(\boldsymbol{A})^2, the criterion of Section 7.4.2.1.

Example. Take J=3 types and two candidate panels of three genes with unit variances (Figure 9). In panel A the three genes have type means (4,2,2), (4,2,0) and (2,1,4); in panel B, (2,4,2), (0,2,4) and (0,2,3). With independent genes, panel A wins on the three criteria (n_i=1, orthonormal \boldsymbol{K}: \det I=116/3 against 104/3, \lambda_{\min}=3.18 against 2.76, \operatorname{tr}I^{-1}=23/58 against 23/52). A correlation of 0.8 between genes 1 and 3 of panel A raises \det I to 60, so D still prefers A, but lowers \lambda_{\min} to 2.05 and raises \operatorname{tr}I^{-1} to 47/90, so E and A prefer B. The correlation sharpens one contrast and blurs the other: the ellipse shrinks in area and lengthens. A univariate screen sees neither change, since the marginal law of each gene is the same in both cases.

This objective needs \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} on the candidate genes, hence the covariance estimation of 3.2 on a shortlist that tier (ii) has already produced. The search itself (greedy exchange, NSGA-II) and its settings are in S6.

7.4.5 Pareto search

AutoGeneS optimises two mean-only objectives with a genetic algorithm (Section 1.2). For DeCovarT the objectives are \kappa_2(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}) (mean geometry) and the average pairwise overlap \bar\varpi of the type laws \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j) restricted to \mathcal{G} (Melnykov et al. 2012, 2024). The overlap and the other separation measures (Hellinger, Bhattacharyya, Jeffreys, affine-invariant distance) are defined in 4.2; unlike the AutoGeneS objectives they use both means and covariances. A Pareto front of non-dominated panels is reported instead of one weighted score (Mersmann 2024); the planned optimiser is NSGA-II via mco::nsga2(), with genes encoded as a mask in [0,1]^{|\mathcal{G}_0|} and thresholded to a target size.

Note 5: A third objective specific to DeCovarT (proposal)

The robust D- or E-criterion of Equation 37 is a third objective, best used to choose among non-dominated panels. The two kinds of criteria need not agree: overlap measures how well the type laws can be told apart, Fisher information how well \boldsymbol{p} can be estimated. None of the reviewed methods uses the information for \boldsymbol{p} to choose genes (Table 1).

7.4.6 Seeds and Markov boundaries

A panel can also grow from a few seeds (strong markers, genes with a large contribution to I_{\mathcal{G}}) by their neighbours in a fitted graphical model of one type. A Markov blanket of gene g is any set that makes g conditionally independent of the other genes; a Markov boundary is a minimal blanket. For a positive distribution the boundary is unique and equals the neighbour set of g in the minimal undirected I-map (Pearl 1988; Koller and Friedman 2009). In a Gaussian graphical model these are the genes g' with \omega_{gg'}\ne0 in \boldsymbol{\Omega}_j (Bolin et al. 2026), if the fitted graph is taken as the minimal I-map. The construction uses undirected separation; directed d-separation, with its colliders, belongs to DAGs and is a different operation (Figure 10). Boundary expansion can reintroduce collinear means, so the expanded set returns to the Pareto stage.

Genes that change neighbourhood between types (differential networks, INDEED, D-trace, cooperative penalties) are a further source of candidates. Their theory is in 3.3, joint and differential networks; on one specimen their permutation nulls are technical nulls (Warning 1).

7.5 Continuous states

Many tissues, gastruloids included, are continua rather than discrete types. A J-column signature is then a piecewise approximation of an archetype geometry (Hart et al. 2015) or a potency axis (Gulati et al. 2020), and the condition number of the means is large by construction (1). Scores along inferred latent axes, and Fisher information evaluated on continuous components, are open directions; hierarchical panels (lineage, then subtype) remain the pragmatic choice (Wang et al. 2019).

7.6 Mechanistic priors

Prior-knowledge networks can annotate a statistically chosen panel or add soft coverage constraints. CARNIVAL contextualises a prior network from expression footprints by integer programming (Liu et al. 2019); CORNETO estimates a shared backbone plus type-specific edges across samples (Rodriguez-Mier et al. 2025). Their outputs depend on the prior network and are hypotheses; they do not replace the criteria of Section 7.4. CardamomOT makes the same point about its own input: the selected gene set acts as prior information (Maugé & Ventre 2026, p. 27).

8 Appendix: concentration results in MEAD and DECALS

MEAD. MEAD’s asymptotics are of another kind than those of Section 4.2.1. Its central limit theorem runs across genes (G\to\infty), not across cells, under local dependence: the noise of most genes forms a dependency graph of bounded degree (Assumption 4, PDF p. 11) (Xie et al. 2026). The normal approximation is “Theorem 2.7 of Chen and Shao” (Lemma S4, supplement pp. S16–S17, PDF pp. 46–47) (Chen & Shao 2004) TODO-cite: Chen & Shao 2004, Normal approximation under local dependence, Ann. Probab. 32(3A):1985-2028; no key in the bibs.

Lemma 1 (Normal approximation under local dependence)

For W=\sum_{g\in M}Z_g with \operatorname{E}W^2=1, \operatorname{E}Z_g=0, \operatorname{E}\lvert Z_g\rvert^{\nu}\le\vartheta^{\nu} and maximal degree d_{\max}, MEAD prints \sum_z\lVert\mathbb{P}(W\le z)-\Phi(z)\rVert\le75\,d_{\max}^{5(\nu-1)}\lvert M\rvert\,\vartheta^{\nu}. As printed, the range of \nu is not stated, and a supremum over z is presumably meant.

Assumption 5b (PDF p. 11) asks for uniformly bounded moments of order above 4 of the bulk data, the reference data and the platform ratios. Fourth moments are more than a central limit theorem for a mean needs: MEAD’s estimator and its sandwich variance contain products of noise terms, and the proof bounds their covariances (PDF p. 40), which takes fourth moments. RNA-Sieve, by contrast, needs a finite per-cell variance for its central limit theorem across cells, and boundedness for its tail.

DECALS. Theorem 1 of DECALS assumes that the noise terms of the bulk “are sub-exponential random variables” and states that this “includes the negative binomial distribution that is often used to model read counts from RNA-seq data” (Cai et al. 2024, supplement p. 22). The paper gives no derivation; Equation 14 supplies one. Its Lemma S3 (supplement p. 23) is property (ii) of Note 1: the moments of a mean-zero sub-exponential variable satisfy (\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert^{\nu})^{1/\nu}\le\eta_2\nu for all \nu\ge1. Eq. S15 (supplement p. 26) applies Lemma S3 to the scaled noise Z_{gj}=\tilde\mu_{gj}\xi_{gi}/\sqrt{\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert}, with \xi_{gi} the noise of gene g in bulk i and \lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert the number of signature genes: \operatorname{E}\lvert Z_{gj}\rvert^{\nu}\le\bigl(\eta_2\tilde\mu_{gj}\,\nu/\sqrt{\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert}\bigr)^{\nu} for every \nu\ge2. This moment bound feeds their central limit theorem across genes, Lemma S4, the same result as Lemma 1. DECALS’s norm in Lemma S2 is the moment form \sup_{\nu\ge1}\nu^{-1}(\operatorname{E}\lvert X\rvert^{\nu})^{1/\nu}, the smallest \eta_2 of property (ii). It equals Equation 13 up to an absolute factor. DECALS cites the equivalences as “Proposition 2.7.1 in Vershynin (2018)”, the first edition; the numbering in Note 1 follows the second edition.

Dependent genes (Zhang & Li). DECALS’s Lemma S2 (supplement p. 23) is Theorem 1 of Zhang & Li, cited as a 2022 preprint TODO-cite: Zhang & Li, Bernstein inequality for dependent sub-exponential variables on a dependency network, J. Comput. Graph. Stat., doi:10.1080/10618600.2024.2421246 (cited by DECALS as the 2022 preprint arXiv:2205.10672); the theorem number in the published version is still to be checked.

Theorem 6 (Bernstein inequality on a dependency graph)

For \lvert M\rvert dependent mean-zero sub-exponential Y_g with dependency graph \mathcal{H}=(M,\mathcal{E}), an edge joining two dependent variables, maximal degree d_{\max} and \bar\chi_G of Equation 30,

\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\sum_{g\in M}Y_g\ge t\Bigr) \le \bar\chi_G\exp\Bigl[-\gamma\min\Bigl\{\frac{t^{2}}{\bar\chi_G^{2}\sum_{g}\lVert Y_g\rVert_{\psi_1}^{2}},\ \frac{t}{\bar\chi_G\max_g\lVert Y_g\rVert_{\psi_1}}\Bigr\}\Bigr]. \tag{39}

With no edge, d_{\max}=0, \lvert\mathcal{E}\rvert=0 and \bar\chi_G=1: the one-sided form of Equation 16 (our remark). A gene network of bounded degree, as DECALS assumes in its Theorem 1, costs a constant factor in the prefactor and in the exponent. In the module of Section 4.2.1, \bar\chi_G=\min(7,8.26)=7. Unlike Theorem 5, this bound keeps the unknown absolute constant \gamma, so it gives the shape of the module tail but no threshold.
